newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economy's fourth-quarter growth revised down.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economy's fourth-quarter growth revised down.

text.p: Weaker inventory-building caused the economy to grow more slowly in the fourth quarter of last year than previously thought, the Commerce Department said on Friday.

The nation's gross domestic product expanded at a 3.9 percent annual rate in the three months ended Dec. 31, instead of the 4.7 percent pace estimated a month ago, the department said in its first revision of fourth-quarter national economic activity.

The revised estimate for fourth-quarter GDP performance was roughly in line with forecasts by Wall Street economists. They had predicted it would be scaled back to a 4.1 percent annual rate of increase.
The revised rate, however, still reflected a strong pace of economic activity as the year ended.

GDP grew during the final three months of 1996 at nearly twice the 2.1 percent rate posted in the third quarter. The revised figure reflects additional information, especially on December inventories, that the department did not have available when it made its first estimate a month ago.
"The downward revision to real GDP was more than accounted for by the downward revision to inventory investment," the Commerce Department said.
It said that while it had assumed a sharp slowdown in inventory building during December, in fact there was a selloff of stocks that had the effect of reducing GDP growth.
GDP measures the value of all goods and services produced by workers and capital within a country's borders.

Despite the weaker figure for fourth-quarter GDP, the revised report showed the economy had considerable momentum as last year ended. The quarterly GDP figure will be revised a final time a month from now.

For example, consumer spending -- which fuels two-thirds of national economic activity -- was revised upward modestly to show an annual rate of increase of $39.8 billion, instead of $38.8 billion as previously estimated.

Before the revised report was released, analysts pointed out that even if lower inventories put a dent in fourth-quarter growth, it still might provide a bounce for the first quarter as manufacturers power up to replenish stocks.

On Thursday the Commerce Department reported that new orders for manufactured durable goods increased strongly in January by 3.6 percent -- about twice the increase economists had expected -- with broad-based gains for everything from machinery to airplanes.
Two inflation measures in the GDP report were left unchanged, reflecting a slowing pace of price changes as 1996 ended instead of higher costs.
The implicit price deflator advanced at a 1.4 percent annual rate in the fourth quarter compared with 1.7 percent in the third quarter.
The fixed-weights measure of price changes gained at a 1.8 percent rate in last year's final quarter, down from 2 percent in the third quarter.
Another sign of the economy's strength came from the government's revision upward in its estimate of business investment in new plants and equipment.
Instead of growing at an $8 billion annual rate, as estimated a month ago, business investment climbed at a $10.4 billion annual rate in the final three months last year.
